sources.supports: cash declaration threshold, scope and penalties

money-and-cost.rate_and_date: A$1 = 0.6293 EUR (Reserve Bank of Australia, 30 October 2026)
money-and-cost.cash_card_notes: Cash declaration: French Customs requires anyone carrying cash, bearer negotiable instruments, prepaid cards or gold worth 10,000 euros or more (or the equivalent) to declare it, whether or not they live in France. 10,000 euros is about A$15,891 at the RBA rate of 30 October 2026 (A$1 = EUR 0.6293). Amounts of 50,000 euros or more also need proof of where the money came from. Declare online (the DALIA service, up to 30 days ahead) or on a paper form. Failing to declare can bring a fine of up to 50% of the amount and seizure of the cash. The page names Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon as an overseas collectivity, where Article L722-6 applies with its own dedicated form.

items.text: Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon is an overseas collectivity of France. France's national drug penalties are: Using any narcotic, cannabis included, is banned even in private and for recreation. The usual response is a fixed fine of EUR 200 (about A$318 at the RBA rate of 30 October 2026, A$1 = EUR 0.6293); a court can impose up to 1 year in prison and EUR 3,750 (about A$5,959). Service-Public's page is written for France as a whole; it does not say how each collectivity applies it.

Under Article 74 of the French Constitution each overseas collectivity has its own statute that sets out how national law applies there. Which parts of the drug-use rules apply here has not been confirmed from the statute.
